Photograph: Mark Richardson/Alamy Prisons and probation Electronic tagging system failing to alert authorities of probation breaches, watchdog warns Probation inspector for England and Wales says ‘clunky’ system needs huge increase in staff Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.45 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The electronic tagging system that will be relied upon to monitor thousands of offenders released early from prison is failing to alert the authorities of potential breaches of conditions, a watchdog has warned. Martin Jones, HM inspector of probation in England and Wales, said the system relied on hard-pressed police and probation officers looking up individual cases and then deciding whether potential breaches needed to be investigated further. He said it needed to be updated to send alerts to the authorities if a former inmate breached an exclusion zone from which they were banned. His demand comes after the government announced that up to 5,000 prisoners would be released from 1 October to ease the prison overcrowding crisis. At present, there are 86,500 people behind bars with 2,400 spare places. Andy Burnham paused the scheme last month and on Tuesday he announced plans to exclude prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sexual abuse offences and grooming, reducing the number of releases by 1,000. Killers and domestic abusers will still be eligible for early release, the Ministry of Justice has confirmed. Line graph showing projected prison population in 2030 The prime minister has assured the public that offenders will face tighter community supervision, including new GPS monitoring. Jones, in an interview with the Guardian, said he had recently launched an inspection of offender tagging, and had seen that the system was coming under strain and needed to be upgraded to “minimise the risk to the public”. “Some of the systems are pretty clunky and it’s far too reliant on people looking for the information rather than the information being fed or pushed to practitioners as a matter of course,” he said. “Tagging has potential to improve public perception of victims’ safety. But only if it used properly and if there is a wider system and enough staff to support that. If not, there is a risk that you give false assurances to the public.” The number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled to 28,700 in five years, and the number of newly tagged each year is expected to rise to 22,000 from 2027. Jones said this expansion needed a huge increase in staff to monitor offenders. The prison population has fallen under Labour An early review of Jones’s inspection, across six regions in England, found: Probation officers wrongly assuming they would be notified about breaches of exclusion zones, when they were required to conduct a specific search. Data was not being actively monitored or analysed to reduce risk to the public. “Significant complexity” was involved in managing the monitoring process, leaving probation officers “overwhelmed and disengaged” by the volume of correspondence. Jones said: “My concern is this: have the processes and the system kept apace with the number of people being tagged? Because ultimately all tagging gives you is information about where somebody is at a particular point in time. You are relying on having sufficient police officers and probation officers to look at that information and make a decision about how it informs your picture on the activities of that individual.” Last month the National Audit Office found that the rapid expansion of electronic tagging to reduce pressure on prisons would put public safety at risk unless there were robust improvements. ‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release scheme Read more Jones also called for the government to ensure that there were enough staff in approved premises , which are hostels set up to monitor 2,000 of the most serious offenders when they are first released from prison. “Our research shows that approved premises work. [They] are extremely effective at managing people after their initial release from custody. What a missed opportunity if those premises cannot remain open because of our insufficient staff,” he said. After a review of the plans, rapists and serious child sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators, will no longer be eligible for the early release scheme. But those given custodial sentences for domestic abuse, and criminals guilty of manslaughter, will still be eligible to be freed halfway through their sentence. Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has apologised to families affected, saying they were “carrying the can from previous failures”. He acknowledged the proposals had “created harm” for those grieving, such as the wife of PC Andrew Harper, Lissie. “I would express how angry I am, too, at being in a situation where we’re having to make significant changes that do have real impacts on people’s lives, so that we are able to have a functioning prison system,” he said. Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, said her family was “paying the price” after learning her son’s killers remained eligible for early release under the plans. Sarah Champion, the Labour MP for Rotherham, has written to Burnham, telling him that victims would “remain in a state of fear and limbo” unless domestic abusers were no longer included in the early release scheme. She told the prime minister: “I fully support the government’s ambitious goal to reduce violence against women and girls and tackle serious sexual offences. However, without reinstating the exemption to the early release scheme, I fail to see how that is possible.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation UK criminal justice England Wales news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity About 1,000 fewer prisoners to get early release as Burnham tightens rules PM to tighten early release rules but men jailed over PC Harper’s death can be freed More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time Burnham stirs up political row with review of release plans for violent criminals Lack of safeguards over prisoners’ early release puts abuse victims at risk, Lammy warned Prison officers given more training to avoid being manipulated into illicit relationships with inmates Tens of thousands of prisoners in England and Wales at risk of cell fires ‘Missed opportunities’ to prevent woman’s death in prison cell fire, inquest finds Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Ashish Gurung/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Desperate rescue attempts continue in Nepal to reach hundreds thought to be trapped Death toll from unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris now stands at more than 900. Plus, was it a mistake to take away Pluto’s planet status? Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Martin Belam Mon 31 Aug 2026 06.34 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 07.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Rescue teams are working to reach hundreds of people feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of half a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal as more than 900 workers were reported missing after the devastating flash floods. The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has risen to 903 people, with 16 reported dead on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves. How large is the rescue operation? Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers. China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers. The Red Cross has ‌estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts linked to the effects of the climate crisis. Why has the disaster sparked a racism row in Australia? A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards missing Australians . Most of them were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians. US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan and UAE View image in fullscreen A wide view of the northern part of the strait of Hormuz, showing the islands of Hormuz (R), Larak (C), and Qeshm (L). Photograph: Satellite image ©2020 Maxar Tech/AFP/Getty Images Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates after the US attacked Iranian rocket launchers in the strait of Hormuz, the first such hostilities in a month. The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks. The latest exchange of fire was sparked late on Sunday by a US attack on the island of Larak in the strait. Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and ​would be met with “punishment” from ‌Tehran. What has Donald Trump claimed US forces are doing? Hours after the attacks, the US president, Donald Trump, claimed in a social media post that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens” but gave no further details. The White House and ⁠the US defense department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Attacking Kharg, which handled 90% of ⁠Iran’s oil exports before the war, would severely disrupt the Islamic republic’s energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy. Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates View image in fullscreen The Lake Ontario sign. Photograph: Carlos Osorio/Reuters Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel at the weekend over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting an AI video depicting him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA. The Wendat Nation grand chief, Pierre Picard, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said. Trump ‘border czar’ denies Milo Yiannopoulos was deported quickly to spare him from ICE detention Milo Yiannopoulos after his arrest by federal immigration agents. Photograph: Department of Homeland Security/Reuters The White House “border czar”, Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that deporting the British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment . Homan said it was his understanding Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July. He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.” In other news … View image in fullscreen NBC’s Kristen Welker. Photograph: Jim Bourg/Reuters Donald Trump ⁠said NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face “rebuke or punishment” from the FCC after she described the success record of political candidates whom the president had endorsed as “mixed”. Ghislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn her conviction for her involvement in Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse of girls and young women, experts say, bar a presidential pardon. At least eight people have died off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus after a ferry capsized . Nearly 20 people are still missing. The Trump administration is shuttering ⁠two of the three US Department of Agriculture research projects studying cyclospora after the foodborne parasite has ⁠sickened tens of thousands of Americans during the summer. Michigan’s Democratic US senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed apologized to the state’s Jewish Democratic Caucus for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March , which he tied to Israel’s actions in the Middle East. Stat of the day: Discount gas stations praised by Trump sold $4m of stolen fuel, lawsuit claims View image in fullscreen A flag flies at Freedom Fuel Network gas station. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP Mansfield Oil Company of Gainesville is suing KRSM and its president, Syed Kazmi, for allegedly picking up nearly $4m of fuel and not paying for it. KRSM sold some of the fuel to stations that are part of the Freedom Fuel Network, promoted by the Trump administration when drivers were facing higher oil prices amid the war with Iran.
